units.density: g/cm3 for solids and liquids near room temperature; g/L for gases at 0 °C and 1 atm

sources.weights: IUPAC/CIAAW standard atomic weights 2021 (Prohaska et al., Pure Appl. Chem. 94, 573, 2022), as listed on iupac.qmul.ac.uk/AtWt; intervals shown as conventional values. Mass numbers in brackets: longest-lived isotope (see halfLives).
sources.isotopes: NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions (IUPAC representative isotopic compositions), physics.nist.gov.
sources.halfLives: Longest-lived isotopes: Wikipedia, "List of elements by stability of isotopes" (NUBASE2020 values); seaborgium and hassium from "Isotopes of seaborgium" and "Isotopes of hassium"; half-lives of naturally radioactive isotopes from Wikipedia, "List of nuclides".
sources.configurations: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, ground levels of the neutral atoms (exceptions to Madelung filling as measured; Rf onward predicted).
sources.ie1: NIST Atomic Spectra Database, "Ground levels and ionization energies for the neutral atoms" (physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl), fetched 2026-10-20.
sources.en: Revised Pauling electronegativities (A. L. Allred, 1961) as tabulated in the CRC Handbook; same values as the site's Chemistry Ladder.
sources.radius: B. Cordero et al., "Covalent radii revisited", Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832; same table as the site's Chemistry Ladder.
sources.physical: Melting point, boiling point, density and state: Wikipedia, "List of chemical elements" (values from the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics and the element articles), cross-checked against the CRC rows of Wikipedia's data pages for melting points, boiling points and densities; differences over 3% (5% for density) are noted.
sources.crust: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, "Abundance of elements in the earth's crust and in the sea", via Wikipedia's "Abundances of the elements (data page)", cross-checked with a second listed source.
sources.spectra: NIST Handbook of Basic Atomic Spectroscopic Data (J. E. Sansonetti and W. C. Martin, NIST), strong-line tables, neutral-atom (I) lines 380–750 nm in air, with NIST's relative intensities; spot-checked against the NIST pages.
sources.discovery: Element articles and "Timeline of chemical element discoveries" on Wikipedia, with IUPAC/IUPAP Joint Working Party reports for the superheavy elements.
sources.text: Names, uses, facts and safety notes written for the Teddy Rook Book from the element articles on Wikipedia and USGS mineral commodity summaries; reviewed for accuracy.

notes.layout: La and Ac sit in group 3 (block d) and Ce–Lu, Th–Lr form the f-block rows 9 and 10, as on the site's Chemistry Ladder. IUPAC's 2021 provisional report favors Lu and Lr in group 3; both layouts are in use.
notes.weights: For elements whose atomic weight varies in nature (H, Li, B, C, N, O, Mg, Si, S, Cl, Ar, Br, Tl, Pb) IUPAC gives an interval; value and text are the conventional values. CIAAW revised Zr (91.222), Gd (157.249) and Lu (174.96669) in 2024; the 2021 values are used here.
notes.radius: Covalent single-bond radii (Cordero 2008). No values exist for Bk and heavier elements.
notes.en: No Pauling values are tabulated for He, Ne, Ar, Rn, Pm, Eu, Tb, Yb, or for elements after Lr; Kr and Xe values come from their compounds.
notes.ie1: Pr, Pa, Fm and Md are NIST's semi-empirical estimates; values from Rf on are theoretical only and left null.
notes.spectra: Neutral-atom lines only. Fine-structure components closer than 0.02 nm are merged (strongest kept). At most the 40 strongest lines are kept. i = rel / strongest visible line. Intensities are NIST's relative estimates for a typical light source and are only roughly comparable between elements.
notes.unknowns: Null means not measured. Predicted values appear only in notes, never in number fields.
notes.halfLives: For the heaviest elements the longest-lived isotope is uncertain and new isotopes may be found.
notes.configurations: Exceptions (measured): Cr, Cu, Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, La, Ce, Gd, Pt, Au, Ac, Th, Pa, U, Np, Cm, Lr. From Rf (104) on, configurations are predicted.

elements.name: Hydrogen

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Robert Boyle made the gas in 1671 without knowing it was an element; Antoine Lavoisier named it in 1783.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek hydro (water) and genes (forming), because it burns to make water.
elements.found: Most hydrogen on Earth is locked up in water and in living things; free hydrogen gas is rare here, but hydrogen makes up most of the Sun and stars.
uses: Fuel cells that turn hydrogen into electricity
elements.fact: Hydrogen is the lightest and most common element in the universe: about three out of every four grams of ordinary matter.
elements.safety: The gas burns very easily and can explode when mixed with air.

elements.name: Helium

melt.note: Does not freeze at normal pressure; solid helium needs about 25 atmospheres.

discovery.by: Pierre Janssen and Norman Lockyer; William Ramsay
discovery.where: Seen in sunlight during an eclipse (India) and from England; found on Earth in London in 1895
discovery.note: It was spotted as a yellow line in the Sun's spectrum 27 years before anyone collected it on Earth.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek helios, the Sun, where it was first detected.
elements.found: Collected from natural gas wells, where it builds up underground from the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium.
uses: Filling party balloons and weather balloons
Cooling the magnets in hospital MRI scanners
A safe, non-burning gas for blimps
elements.fact: Helium is the only element that will not freeze at normal pressure, no matter how cold it gets.

elements.name: Lithium

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Found in the mineral petalite; William Thomas Brande and Humphry Davy first freed the metal by electricity.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek lithos, stone, because it was found in a mineral rather than in plants.
elements.found: Mined from hard-rock minerals such as spodumene and pumped as salty brine from dry lake beds.
uses: Rechargeable batteries for phones, laptops and electric cars
elements.fact: Lithium is the lightest metal; it is so light that it floats on water (while reacting with it).
elements.safety: Reacts with water to make flammable hydrogen.

elements.name: Beryllium

discovery.note: Found as an oxide in beryl and emerald; Friedrich Wöhler and Antoine Bussy isolated the metal in 1828.

elements.nameOrigin: From beryl, the gemstone mineral it was found in.
elements.found: Mined mainly from the minerals bertrandite and beryl; emerald and aquamarine are gem forms of beryl.
uses: Windows for X-ray tubes, since X-rays pass right through it
Light, stiff parts for aircraft and satellites
Springs and non-sparking tools made of beryllium copper
elements.fact: The mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope are made of gold-coated beryllium.
elements.safety: Its dust is toxic to breathe.

elements.name: Boron

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.by: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard; Humphry Davy
discovery.note: Borax, a boron compound, was used for centuries before the element was isolated.

elements.nameOrigin: From borax, the mineral it was isolated from (from the Arabic buraq).
elements.found: Mined as borate minerals such as borax, mostly from dry lake deposits in Turkey and California.
uses: Heat-resistant borosilicate glass (lab glass and baking dishes)
elements.fact: Boron is the element that makes some lab glassware and baking dishes tough enough to go from cold to hot without cracking.

spectrum.note: NIST lists no strong visible lines for neutral boron; its strong lines are ultraviolet.

elements.name: Carbon

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

melt.note: Does not melt at normal pressure; it turns straight from solid to gas (sublimes).

boil.note: Sublimes (turns straight to gas) at normal pressure; sources give about 3,900–4,300 K.

discovery.note: Known since prehistoric times as charcoal and soot; Antoine Lavoisier listed it as an element in 1789.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin carbo, charcoal.
elements.found: Found everywhere: in all living things, in coal, oil and natural gas, in limestone rock, and in the air as carbon dioxide.
uses: Diamonds for jewelry and cutting tools
Steel, which is iron with a little carbon
Fuels such as coal, gasoline and natural gas
elements.fact: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon; they differ only in how the atoms are arranged.

elements.name: Nitrogen

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: He called it "noxious air" because a candle would not burn in it.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek nitron (saltpeter or soda) and genes (forming), since it is part of saltpeter.
elements.found: Makes up about 78 percent of the air; it is also in all proteins and DNA.
uses: Liquid nitrogen for freezing and storing samples
Filling food packages so chips stay fresh
elements.fact: Every breath you take is mostly nitrogen, which goes in and comes back out unchanged.

elements.name: Oxygen

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Scheele made it first but published late; Priestley found it independently in 1774, and Antoine Lavoisier named it.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek oxys (sharp or acid) and genes (forming); Lavoisier wrongly thought all acids contain it.
elements.found: About 21 percent of the air, most of the weight of water, and nearly half the weight of Earth's rocks.
elements.fact: Oxygen is the most common element in Earth's crust by weight, mostly bound into rocks and sand.
elements.safety: Pure oxygen makes fires burn far more fiercely.

elements.name: Fluorine

discovery.note: Chemists knew the element existed for decades but could not free it; Moissan won the 1906 Nobel Prize for doing so.

elements.nameOrigin: From the mineral fluorite (Latin fluere, to flow), which was used to help metal ores melt.
elements.found: Mined in the minerals fluorite and fluorapatite.
uses: Fluoride in toothpaste and drinking water to protect teeth
elements.fact: Fluorine is the most electronegative element: it pulls electrons harder than any other.
elements.safety: The gas is extremely toxic and reactive.

elements.name: Neon

discovery.note: Found by boiling off liquefied air and looking at the leftover gases.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek neos, new.
elements.found: A tiny part of the air (about 18 parts per million), separated from liquefied air.
elements.fact: Only pure neon gives a neon sign its red-orange glow; other colors come from other gases or coated glass tubes.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Sodium

discovery.note: Davy freed it by passing electricity through melted lye (sodium hydroxide).

elements.nameOrigin: From soda; the symbol Na comes from the Latin natrium.
elements.found: Common in rock salt and seawater as sodium chloride, and in many minerals.
elements.fact: The bright yellow color of a candle flame with salt sprinkled in comes from sodium's two strong lines near 589 nm.

elements.name: Magnesium

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.where: Edinburgh, Scotland; isolated in London, England, in 1808
discovery.note: Black recognized it as a new element; Davy first isolated the metal.

elements.nameOrigin: From Magnesia, a district in Greece where its minerals were found.
elements.found: Taken from seawater and from minerals such as dolomite and magnesite.
uses: Light alloys for car wheels, laptops and bikes
elements.fact: Every chlorophyll molecule, which makes plants green, has a magnesium atom at its center.
elements.safety: Burns with a blinding white flame that water does not put out.

elements.name: Aluminum

discovery.note: Friedrich Wöhler made purer aluminum in 1827.

elements.nameOrigin: From alum, a salt used in dyeing (Latin alumen); Americans say aluminum, most others say aluminium.
elements.found: The most common metal in Earth's crust; it is refined from bauxite ore.
elements.fact: In the 1850s aluminum was so costly it was treated like a precious metal; the small pyramid capping the Washington Monument (1884) is made of it.

elements.name: Silicon

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Berzelius made fairly pure silicon in 1823–24.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin silex (flint).
elements.found: The second most common element in Earth's crust, in sand, quartz and most rocks.
elements.fact: Silicon Valley in California is named after the element used in nearly every computer chip.

elements.name: Phosphorus

melt.note: White phosphorus; red phosphorus behaves differently.

discovery.note: Brand made it by boiling down large amounts of urine; it is the first element with a known discoverer.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek phosphoros, light-bearer, because white phosphorus glows in the dark.
elements.found: Mined as phosphate rock; it is also in bones, teeth and DNA.
elements.fact: White phosphorus glows faintly in air as it slowly reacts with oxygen.
elements.safety: White phosphorus is toxic and catches fire by itself in air.

elements.name: Sulfur

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Known since ancient times; Antoine Lavoisier recognized it as an element in 1777.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin sulpur.
elements.found: Found as yellow crystals near volcanoes and hot springs, and recovered from natural gas and oil.
uses: Making sulfuric acid, the most-produced industrial chemical
elements.fact: The rotten-egg smell people blame on sulfur comes from compounds like hydrogen sulfide; pure sulfur barely smells.

elements.name: Chlorine

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Humphry Davy showed in 1810 that it was an element.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek chloros, pale green, the color of the gas.
elements.found: Mostly in seawater and rock salt as chloride.
uses: Disinfecting drinking water and swimming pools
elements.fact: Table salt is half chlorine by atom count, yet chlorine gas on its own is poisonous.
elements.safety: The gas is toxic to breathe.

elements.name: Argon

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Found because nitrogen from air weighed slightly more than nitrogen made from chemicals.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek argos, lazy or idle, because it does not react.
elements.found: Almost 1 percent of the air, separated from liquefied air.
elements.fact: Argon is the third most common gas in the air, far more common than carbon dioxide.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Potassium

discovery.note: It was the first metal ever isolated by electricity.

elements.nameOrigin: From potash (pot ashes); the symbol K comes from the Latin kalium.
elements.found: In minerals such as sylvite and in seawater; plants need it to grow.
elements.fact: Bananas are famous for potassium, but potatoes and beans have even more.

elements.name: Calcium

discovery.note: Lime (calcium oxide) had been used since ancient times.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin calx, lime.
elements.found: In limestone, chalk, marble and gypsum, and in shells, bones and teeth.
elements.fact: Calcium is the most common metal in the human body; most of it is in the skeleton.

elements.name: Scandium

discovery.note: Its properties matched those Dmitri Mendeleev predicted for "eka-boron."

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin Scandia, Scandinavia.
elements.found: Spread thinly through many minerals; it is usually recovered as a by-product of other mining.
uses: Light aluminum-scandium alloys for bike frames and sports gear
elements.fact: Scandium helped prove Mendeleev right: he had predicted its weight and properties years before it was found.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Titanium

discovery.note: Martin Heinrich Klaproth named it in 1795; fairly pure metal was first made in 1910.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Titans of Greek myth.
elements.found: Mined as the minerals ilmenite and rutile, often from beach sands.
uses: White pigment in paint, paper and toothpaste (titanium dioxide)
Hip and knee replacements and dental implants
elements.fact: Titanium is about as strong as many steels but weighs only a little more than half as much.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Vanadium

discovery.by: Andrés Manuel del Río; Nils Gabriel Sefström
discovery.where: Mexico City, Mexico; rediscovered in Sweden in 1830
discovery.note: Del Río was wrongly told he had found chromium; Sefström rediscovered it and named it.

elements.nameOrigin: From Vanadís, a name of the Norse goddess Freyja, for its many colorful compounds.
elements.found: Mined from magnetite ores and recovered from some oils and coal ash.
uses: Tough steel for tools and car parts
Large flow batteries for storing power
elements.fact: Henry Ford used vanadium steel in the Model T because it was strong yet light.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Chromium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Found in the red mineral crocoite; he isolated the metal in 1798.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek chroma, color, for its brightly colored compounds.
elements.found: Mined as the mineral chromite.
elements.fact: Rubies are red and emeralds green partly because of small amounts of chromium.
elements.safety: Some chromium compounds (hexavalent chromium) are toxic and cause cancer.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Manganese

discovery.note: Carl Wilhelm Scheele and Torbern Bergman had recognized it was a new element.

elements.nameOrigin: From magnesia, via Latin and Italian (the ore came from the Magnesia region).
elements.found: Mined as pyrolusite and other ores; the ocean floor is dotted with manganese nodules.
elements.fact: Ancient cave painters used manganese oxide as black paint.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Iron

discovery.note: Known since prehistoric times; the oldest iron objects were made from meteorites.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Anglo-Saxon iren; the symbol Fe comes from the Latin ferrum.
elements.found: Mined as hematite and magnetite; Earth's core is mostly iron.
uses: Steel for buildings, bridges, cars and tools
Iron in the hemoglobin that carries oxygen in blood
elements.fact: Iron is the most common element in Earth as a whole, because of the planet's iron core.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Cobalt

discovery.note: He showed the blue color in glass came from a new metal, not bismuth.

elements.nameOrigin: From the German Kobold, a goblin; miners blamed goblins for troublesome ores.
elements.found: Mined mostly as a by-product of copper and nickel, much of it in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
uses: Deep blue color for glass and pottery
elements.fact: Vitamin B12 has a cobalt atom at its center.

elements.name: Nickel

discovery.note: Found in an ore that miners called Kupfernickel because it looked like copper but gave none.

elements.nameOrigin: From the German Kupfernickel, "copper demon."
elements.found: Mined from sulfide ores and laterites; much of Earth's nickel is in its core.
elements.fact: A US five-cent coin called a "nickel" is actually 75 percent copper and only 25 percent nickel.
elements.safety: A common cause of skin allergy in jewelry.

elements.name: Copper

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Used for more than 9,000 years; it was one of the first metals people worked.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin cuprum, after the island of Cyprus, an ancient source.
elements.found: Mined from sulfide ores such as chalcopyrite, and sometimes found as pure metal.
elements.fact: The Statue of Liberty is covered in copper; its green color is a thin layer called patina.

elements.name: Zinc

discovery.note: Metalworkers in India and China were producing zinc centuries earlier; Marggraf described how to isolate it.

elements.nameOrigin: From the German Zink, perhaps from Zinke (prong), for the shape of its crystals.
elements.found: Mined as sphalerite (zinc sulfide).
uses: Galvanizing steel to keep it from rusting
elements.fact: A US penny made since 1982 is about 97.5 percent zinc with a thin copper coat.

elements.name: Gallium

discovery.note: Found by its spectrum; it matched Mendeleev's predicted "eka-aluminium."

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin Gallia, France.
elements.found: Recovered in small amounts while processing bauxite (aluminum ore) and zinc ores.
uses: LEDs and laser diodes (gallium nitride and gallium arsenide)
Chips in cell phones and radar
elements.fact: Gallium melts at about 30 °C (86 °F), so a piece will melt in your hand.

elements.name: Germanium

discovery.note: Its properties matched Mendeleev's predicted "eka-silicon."

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin Germania, Germany.
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of zinc ores and coal ash.
uses: Lenses for infrared and night-vision cameras
elements.fact: The first transistors, made in 1947, used germanium rather than silicon.

spectrum.note: NIST's strong lines of neutral germanium are ultraviolet and infrared; the visible ones are from the ion.

elements.name: Arsenic

melt.note: Melts only under pressure (about 1,090 K); at normal pressure it sublimes.

boil.note: Sublimes (turns straight to gas) at normal pressure.

discovery.note: Arsenic compounds were known in ancient times; Albertus Magnus is often credited with isolating it around 1250.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek arsenikon, the yellow mineral orpiment.
elements.found: Found in many sulfide ores and recovered while refining copper and lead.
uses: Gallium arsenide chips in phones and LEDs
elements.fact: Arsenic usually skips the liquid state: at normal pressure it turns straight from solid to gas.
elements.safety: Arsenic and its compounds are poisonous.

spectrum.note: NIST's strong lines of neutral arsenic are ultraviolet and infrared; the visible ones are from the ion.

elements.name: Selenium

melt.note: Gray selenium, the stable form; glassy selenium softens near 453 K.

discovery.by: Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Johan Gottlieb Gahn
discovery.note: Found in sludge from a sulfuric acid factory.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek selene, the Moon (it resembles tellurium, named for Earth).
elements.found: Recovered while refining copper.
uses: Decolorizing glass and making red glass
elements.fact: Selenium's electrical behavior changes when light hits it, which made it useful in early light meters and photocopiers.
elements.safety: Needed in tiny amounts in the diet, but toxic in larger doses.

elements.name: Bromine

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Both found it independently; Balard published first, in 1826.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek bromos, stench, for its sharp smell.
elements.found: Extracted from seawater and from salty brines such as the Dead Sea.
elements.fact: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury.
elements.safety: The liquid and its vapor are toxic and burn skin.

elements.name: Krypton

discovery.note: Found in the last bit of liquefied air left after the rest boiled away.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek kryptos, hidden.
elements.found: A trace gas in the air (about 1 part per million), separated from liquefied air.
uses: Krypton-fluoride lasers used to make computer chips
elements.fact: From 1960 to 1983 the meter was defined by an orange-red line of krypton-86.

elements.name: Rubidium

discovery.note: Found with a spectroscope by its two deep red lines.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin rubidus, deep red, the color of its spectral lines.
elements.found: Recovered from the minerals lepidolite and pollucite.
uses: Atomic clocks, including some GPS satellite clocks
elements.fact: Rubidium melts at about 39 °C (102 °F), just above body temperature.
elements.safety: Reacts violently with water and catches fire in air.

elements.name: Strontium

discovery.where: Britain (from ore mined at Strontian, Scotland)
discovery.note: Humphry Davy isolated the metal in 1808.

elements.nameOrigin: From Strontian, a village in Scotland where its mineral was found.
elements.found: Mined as celestine and strontianite.
elements.fact: Strontium salts give fireworks their brightest crimson reds.

elements.name: Yttrium

discovery.note: Found in a black mineral from the Swedish village of Ytterby; Friedrich Wöhler isolated impure metal in 1828.

elements.nameOrigin: From Ytterby, a village in Sweden.
elements.found: Found with the rare earth elements in minerals such as xenotime and monazite.
uses: Red color in old TV screens and some LEDs
elements.fact: Four elements are named for the same tiny Swedish village: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Zirconium

discovery.note: Found in the gem zircon; Jöns Jacob Berzelius isolated the metal in 1824.

elements.nameOrigin: From zircon, the mineral (possibly from the Persian zargun, gold-colored).
elements.found: Mined as zircon from beach sands.
uses: Tubes that hold nuclear reactor fuel
elements.fact: Some zircon crystals from Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, among the oldest pieces of Earth.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Niobium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: He called it columbium; chemists agreed on the name niobium in 1949.

elements.nameOrigin: From Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth, because it is so similar to tantalum.
elements.found: Mined mostly as pyrochlore, much of it in Brazil.
uses: Stronger steel for pipelines and cars
elements.fact: Niobium-titanium wire carries electricity with no resistance at all when cooled with liquid helium.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Molybdenum

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Peter Jacob Hjelm isolated the metal in 1781.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek molybdos, lead, because its ore was confused with lead ore.
elements.found: Mined as molybdenite, often alongside copper.
uses: Tough "chrome-moly" steel for tools and bike frames
Catalysts that remove sulfur from fuels
elements.fact: Bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into fertilizer for plants need molybdenum to do it.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Technetium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

mostStable.note: Technetium-98 (4.2 million years) lasts almost as long.

discovery.note: Found in a piece of molybdenum foil sent from a cyclotron in Berkeley, California.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek technetos, artificial; it was the first element made by people.
elements.found: Almost none occurs naturally; tiny traces form in uranium ores, and it has been seen in the light of some stars.
uses: Medical scans: technetium-99m is the most widely used medical radioisotope
elements.fact: Finding technetium in stars in 1952 showed that stars make new elements, since it decays too fast to be left over from the Sun's birth.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Ruthenium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Found in residue left after refining platinum ore from the Ural Mountains.

elements.nameOrigin: From Ruthenia, the Latin name for a region including Russia.
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of platinum and nickel mining.
uses: Thin layers inside computer hard drives
elements.fact: Ruthenium was the last of the platinum-group metals to be discovered.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Rhodium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Found in platinum ore from South America; Wollaston found it in 1803 and announced it in 1804.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek rhodon, rose, for the rose color of its salts.
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of platinum and nickel mining, mostly in South Africa.
uses: Bright, hard plating on jewelry and white gold
elements.fact: Rhodium is one of the rarest and often the most expensive of the precious metals.

elements.name: Palladium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Wollaston first sold it anonymously as a "new silver" before revealing he had found it.

elements.nameOrigin: From Pallas, an asteroid discovered in 1802 and named for the Greek goddess Pallas Athena.
elements.found: Mined with platinum and nickel, mainly in Russia and South Africa.
elements.fact: Palladium can soak up hundreds of times its own volume of hydrogen gas.

elements.name: Silver

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Known since ancient times; silver objects date back more than 5,000 years.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Anglo-Saxon seolfor; the symbol Ag comes from the Latin argentum.
elements.found: Mined from silver ores and recovered from lead, zinc and copper ores; sometimes found as pure metal.
elements.fact: Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other metal.

elements.name: Cadmium

discovery.note: Found as an impurity in zinc carbonate.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin cadmia, an old name for zinc ore (calamine).
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of zinc refining.
uses: Bright yellow, orange and red pigments
elements.fact: Artists such as Claude Monet used cadmium yellow paints for their bright, lasting color.
elements.safety: Cadmium and its compounds are toxic.

elements.name: Indium

discovery.by: Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymus Theodor Richter
discovery.note: Found by a bright indigo-blue line in its spectrum.

elements.nameOrigin: From indigo, the color of its brightest spectral line.
elements.found: Recovered mainly as a by-product of zinc refining.
uses: Touchscreens and flat-panel displays (indium tin oxide)
elements.fact: Indium is so soft you can scratch it with a fingernail.

elements.name: Tin

discovery.note: Known since ancient times; mixing it with copper to make bronze began more than 5,000 years ago.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Anglo-Saxon tin; the symbol Sn comes from the Latin stannum.
elements.found: Mined as cassiterite (tin oxide).
elements.fact: Bending a bar of tin makes a faint crackling sound called "tin cry."

elements.name: Antimony

discovery.note: Known since ancient times; an antimony vase from about 3000 BC has been found in what is now Iraq.

elements.nameOrigin: The origin of "antimony" is uncertain; the symbol Sb comes from the Latin stibium.
elements.found: Mined mainly as stibnite (antimony sulfide).
uses: Flame retardants in plastics and fabrics
elements.fact: Ancient Egyptians used powdered stibnite, an antimony mineral, as black eye makeup.
elements.safety: Antimony and its compounds are toxic.

spectrum.note: NIST's strong visible lines of antimony come from the ion, not the neutral atom.

elements.name: Tellurium

discovery.note: Found in gold ore; Martin Heinrich Klaproth confirmed it and named it in 1798.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin tellus, Earth.
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of copper refining; it is one of the rarer elements in Earth's crust.
uses: Making steel and copper easier to machine
elements.fact: People exposed to even small amounts of tellurium can have garlic-smelling breath for weeks.

spectrum.note: NIST's strong visible lines of tellurium come from the ion, not the neutral atom.

elements.name: Iodine

discovery.note: Found while making saltpeter from seaweed ash.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek iodes, violet, the color of its vapor.
elements.found: Taken from underground brines and from deposits in Chile; seaweed concentrates it from seawater.
elements.fact: Your thyroid gland needs iodine to make its hormones, which is why iodine is added to salt.

elements.name: Xenon

discovery.note: Found in the heaviest leftover part of liquefied air.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek xenos, stranger.
elements.found: A very rare gas in air (about 0.09 parts per million), separated from liquefied air.
uses: Bright car headlights and camera flashes
elements.fact: In 1962 Neil Bartlett showed that xenon can form compounds, overturning the idea that noble gases never react.

elements.name: Cesium

discovery.note: Found with a spectroscope in mineral water; the first element discovered by its spectrum.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin caesius, sky blue, for its two blue spectral lines.
elements.found: Mined as the mineral pollucite.
uses: Atomic clocks that define the second
Drilling fluids for oil and gas wells (cesium formate)
elements.fact: The second is defined by cesium-133 atoms: it is exactly 9,192,631,770 waves of the microwave radiation they absorb and give off.

elements.name: Barium

discovery.note: Humphry Davy isolated the metal in London in 1808.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek barys, heavy, because its mineral barite is unusually dense.
elements.found: Mined as barite (barium sulfate).
uses: Drilling mud for oil and gas wells
Barium sulfate for X-ray images of the stomach and intestines
elements.fact: Barium sulfate shows up on X-rays because barium's heavy atoms block X-rays well.

elements.name: Lanthanum

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Found hidden in cerium nitrate; Wilhelm Muthmann and Lothar Weiss isolated the metal in 1904.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek lanthanein, to lie hidden.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in bastnäsite and monazite.
elements.fact: Lanthanum gives the whole lanthanide series its name.

elements.name: Cerium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.by: Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger; Martin Heinrich Klaproth
discovery.note: Found independently in Sweden and Germany.

elements.nameOrigin: From the dwarf planet Ceres, discovered two years earlier.
elements.found: The most abundant rare earth element; mined in bastnäsite and monazite.
uses: Polishing powder for glass and lenses (cerium oxide)
elements.fact: Scraping a lighter flint, an alloy of cerium, other rare earths and iron, throws off sparks of burning metal.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Praseodymium

discovery.note: He split "didymium," thought to be one element, into two: praseodymium and neodymium.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek prasios didymos, green twin, for its green salts.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in bastnäsite and monazite.
uses: Protective goggles for welders and glassblowers
elements.fact: Praseodymium and neodymium were once thought to be a single element called didymium.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Neodymium

discovery.note: Split from "didymium" along with praseodymium.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek neos didymos, new twin.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in bastnäsite and monazite.
uses: The strongest permanent magnets (earbuds, motors, wind turbines)
elements.fact: A neodymium magnet the size of a coin can lift many times its own weight.

elements.name: Promethium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

boil.note: An estimate; it has not been measured directly.

discovery.by: Jacob Marinsky, Lawrence Glendenin and Charles Coryell
discovery.note: Identified in spent fuel from the graphite reactor at Oak Ridge.

elements.nameOrigin: From Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods in Greek myth.
elements.found: Only tiny traces occur naturally, in uranium ores; it is produced in nuclear reactors.
uses: Long-life "atomic batteries" that turn its radiation into electricity
elements.fact: Promethium is the only lanthanide with no stable isotopes.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Samarium

discovery.note: Found in the mineral samarskite.

elements.nameOrigin: From samarskite, a mineral named for Russian mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in monazite and bastnäsite.
uses: Samarium-cobalt magnets that work at high temperatures
elements.fact: Samarium was the first element named, indirectly, after a person.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Europium

discovery.note: He first saw its spectral lines in 1896.

elements.nameOrigin: From the continent of Europe.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths, mostly from bastnäsite.
uses: Red and blue glow in screens and energy-saving bulbs
Glowing marks that help prevent counterfeit banknotes
elements.fact: Europium is the most reactive of the lanthanides and quickly tarnishes in air.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Gadolinium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran isolated a purer oxide in 1886.

elements.nameOrigin: From the mineral gadolinite, named for the Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in monazite and bastnäsite.
elements.fact: Gadolinium is magnetic only when cooled below about 20 °C (68 °F), close to room temperature.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Terbium

discovery.note: The names terbium and erbium got swapped by later chemists.

elements.nameOrigin: From Ytterby, a village in Sweden.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths, mostly from ion-adsorption clays and monazite.
uses: Green glow in screens and fluorescent lamps
elements.fact: Terbium compounds glow bright green under ultraviolet light.

elements.name: Dysprosium

discovery.note: It took him more than 30 tries to separate it.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek dysprositos, hard to get at.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths, especially from ion-adsorption clays.
uses: Helping neodymium magnets keep working when hot (electric cars, wind turbines)
elements.fact: Pure dysprosium was not produced until the 1950s, about 70 years after its discovery.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Holmium

discovery.by: Jacques-Louis Soret and Marc Delafontaine; Per Teodor Cleve
discovery.note: Soret and Delafontaine saw its spectrum in 1878; Cleve isolated its oxide in 1879.

elements.nameOrigin: From Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in monazite and gadolinite.
uses: Pole pieces for the strongest magnets
elements.fact: Holmium has the strongest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Erbium

discovery.note: Found in the mineral gadolinite from Ytterby.

elements.nameOrigin: From Ytterby, a village in Sweden.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in monazite and xenotime.
uses: Boosting light signals in fiber-optic internet cables
Lasers for skin and dental work
elements.fact: Erbium amplifiers in undersea fiber-optic cables help carry the internet across oceans.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Thulium

discovery.note: Separated from erbium oxide.

elements.nameOrigin: From Thule, a mythical land in the far north.
elements.found: Mined in small amounts with the other rare earths in monazite.
elements.fact: Thulium is one of the rarest lanthanides, yet it is more common in Earth's crust than silver or gold.

elements.name: Ytterbium

discovery.note: Found in erbium oxide.

elements.nameOrigin: From Ytterby, a village in Sweden.
elements.found: Mined with the other rare earths in monazite and xenotime.
uses: Fiber lasers for cutting and welding
Experimental atomic clocks, some of the most precise ever built
elements.fact: Ytterbium is one of four elements named after the same Swedish village.

elements.name: Lutetium

discovery.by: Georges Urbain; Carl Auer von Welsbach; Charles James
discovery.where: Paris, France; Vienna, Austria; Durham, New Hampshire
discovery.note: Three chemists found it at nearly the same time.

elements.nameOrigin: From Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris.
elements.found: Mined in small amounts with the other rare earths in monazite.
uses: Detector crystals in PET medical scanners
elements.fact: Lutetium is the last of the lanthanides and the densest of them.

elements.name: Hafnium

discovery.by: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy
discovery.note: Found with X-ray spectroscopy in zirconium ore.

elements.nameOrigin: From Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen.
elements.found: Always found with zirconium, mostly in zircon; separated while making nuclear-grade zirconium.
elements.fact: Hafnium and zirconium are so alike that hafnium hid in zirconium ores for more than 130 years.

elements.name: Tantalum

discovery.note: Werner von Bolton made pure, workable tantalum in 1903.

elements.nameOrigin: From Tantalus of Greek myth, because its oxide can sit in acid without absorbing it, just as Tantalus could not drink the water around him.
elements.found: Mined as tantalite and coltan, much of it in central Africa.
uses: Tiny capacitors in phones and computers
elements.fact: Tantalum resists corrosion so well that it is used in equipment for handling hot acids.

elements.name: Tungsten

discovery.note: Carl Wilhelm Scheele had found its acid in 1781.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Swedish tung sten, heavy stone; the symbol W comes from wolfram.
elements.found: Mined as wolframite and scheelite, mostly in China.
uses: Tungsten carbide drill bits and cutting tools
elements.fact: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal: about 3,422 °C (6,192 °F).

elements.name: Rhenium

discovery.by: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg
discovery.note: It was the last stable element to be discovered.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin Rhenus, the Rhine River.
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of molybdenum from copper ores.
uses: Superalloys for jet engine turbine blades
elements.fact: Rhenium is one of the rarest elements in Earth's crust, rarer even than gold.

elements.name: Osmium

discovery.note: Found with iridium in the black residue left when platinum ore is dissolved.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek osme, smell, for the sharp odor of its oxide.
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of platinum and nickel mining.
uses: Electrical contacts and instrument pivots (in alloys)
Staining samples for electron microscopes (osmium tetroxide)
elements.fact: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element; a cube 10 cm on a side would weigh about 22.6 kg.
elements.safety: Osmium tetroxide, which forms when the powder meets air, is very toxic.

elements.name: Iridium

discovery.note: Found with osmium in platinum residue.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek iris, rainbow, for its colorful salts.
elements.found: Recovered as a by-product of platinum and nickel mining.
uses: Devices for making chlorine and hydrogen
elements.fact: A thin worldwide layer of clay rich in iridium marks the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs.

elements.name: Platinum

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: People in pre-Columbian South America worked platinum long before Europeans described it.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Spanish platina, little silver.
elements.found: Mined mostly in South Africa and Russia.
elements.fact: The kilogram was defined by a platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris until 2019.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Gold

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Known since prehistoric times; some of the oldest gold objects, from Varna, Bulgaria, are about 6,000 years old.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Old English gold; the symbol Au comes from the Latin aurum.
elements.found: Found as nuggets and flakes of pure metal and in quartz veins; mined on every continent except Antarctica.
elements.fact: Gold is so malleable that a single gram can be hammered into a sheet about one square meter in size.

elements.name: Mercury

discovery.note: Known since ancient times; mercury has been found in Egyptian tombs from about 1500 BC.

elements.nameOrigin: From the planet and Roman god Mercury; the symbol Hg comes from the Greek hydrargyros, liquid silver.
elements.found: Mined as cinnabar (mercury sulfide).
elements.fact: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
elements.safety: Mercury vapor and mercury compounds are toxic.

elements.name: Thallium

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Found by a bright green spectral line; Claude-Auguste Lamy isolated the metal in 1862.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek thallos, a green shoot or twig, for its green spectral line.
elements.found: Recovered in small amounts from the dust and residues of zinc, lead and copper smelting.
uses: Infrared detectors and special optical glass
elements.fact: Thallium's single bright green line at 535 nm gave the element its name.
elements.safety: Thallium and its compounds are highly toxic.

elements.name: Lead

weight.note: Varies a little from sample to sample in nature; IUPAC gives an interval, and the conventional value is shown.

discovery.note: Known since ancient times; lead objects more than 8,000 years old have been found.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Anglo-Saxon lead; the symbol Pb comes from the Latin plumbum.
elements.found: Mined mainly as galena (lead sulfide); much lead today is recycled from old batteries.
uses: Shielding against X-rays and gamma rays
elements.fact: The word "plumbing" comes from plumbum, because Romans made water pipes from lead.
elements.safety: Toxic, especially to children's developing brains.

elements.name: Bismuth

mostStable.note: So slow that bismuth is treated as stable for everyday purposes.

discovery.note: Miners and alchemists used bismuth for centuries but often confused it with tin and lead.

elements.nameOrigin: From the old German wismut, possibly "white mass."
elements.found: Recovered mainly as a by-product of lead, copper and tungsten refining.
elements.fact: Bismuth is very slightly radioactive, but its half-life is more than a billion times the age of the universe.

elements.name: Polonium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

discovery.note: Found in pitchblende, a uranium ore, a few months before radium.

elements.nameOrigin: From Poland, Marie Curie's homeland.
elements.found: Only tiny traces occur in uranium ores; it is made in nuclear reactors.
uses: Anti-static brushes and devices for removing dust from film and lenses
Heat sources in some early space probes
elements.fact: Marie Curie named polonium after Poland, which at the time was divided among other countries.

elements.name: Astatine
elements.categoryNote: Classed by some as a halogen or a metal; too little has ever been made to be sure.

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

elements.stateNote: Never seen in bulk; predicted to be a solid.

melt.note: Never measured; too little has been made. Estimated about 575 K.

discovery.by: Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie and Emilio Segrè
discovery.note: Made by bombarding bismuth with alpha particles; traces were later found in nature.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek astatos, unstable.
elements.found: Only fleeting traces exist in uranium and thorium ores; it is made in particle accelerators.
elements.fact: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element; no one has ever seen a visible amount of it.

spectrum.note: NIST lists only two ultraviolet lines for neutral astatine.

elements.name: Radon

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

discovery.by: Ernest Rutherford and Robert B. Owens; Friedrich Ernst Dorn
discovery.note: Rutherford and Owens found a radioactive gas from thorium; Dorn found one from radium in 1900.

elements.nameOrigin: From radium, because it was found as a gas given off by radium.
elements.found: Forms underground from the decay of uranium and can seep into basements.
uses: Once used in cancer radiation treatment
Tracing how air and groundwater move in scientific studies
elements.fact: Radon is the heaviest noble gas found in nature, about seven and a half times as dense as air.
elements.safety: Radioactive; breathing high levels for years raises the risk of lung cancer.

elements.name: Francium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

elements.stateNote: Never seen in bulk; its melting point is estimated to be near room temperature.

melt.note: Never measured; too little has been made. Estimates run from about 281 to 300 K.

discovery.note: Found as a decay product of actinium at the Curie Institute.

elements.nameOrigin: From France, the discoverer's home country.
elements.found: Only fleeting traces exist in uranium and thorium ores.
elements.fact: Francium was the last element discovered in nature rather than made in a laboratory.

spectrum.note: NIST gives no intensities for these lines, so they are drawn equally bright.

elements.name: Radium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

boil.note: An estimate; sources give about 2,000 K.

discovery.note: Marie Curie and André-Louis Debierne isolated the metal in 1910.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Latin radius, ray.
elements.found: Found in tiny amounts in uranium ores.
uses: Once used in glow-in-the-dark watch dials, a practice since stopped
elements.fact: Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive more than a century later.

elements.name: Actinium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Debierne is usually credited, but historians debate his claim; Giesel found it independently in 1902.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek aktis, ray or beam.
elements.found: Found in tiny amounts in uranium ores; made in nuclear reactors.
elements.fact: Actinium is so radioactive that it glows pale blue in the dark.

elements.name: Thorium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Found in a black mineral from Norway, later named thorite.

elements.nameOrigin: From Thor, the Norse god of thunder.
elements.found: Mined mostly from monazite sand; it is more than three times as common as uranium in Earth's crust.
uses: Once used in gas lantern mantles
elements.fact: Thorium decays so slowly that most of the thorium present when Earth formed is still here.

spectrum.note: The 40 strongest visible lines of the neutral atom are shown.

elements.name: Protactinium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.by: Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Göhring; Otto Hahn and Lise Meitner
discovery.note: Fajans and Göhring found a short-lived isotope; Hahn and Meitner found the long-lived one in 1918.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Greek protos (first) plus actinium, because it decays into actinium.
elements.found: Found in tiny amounts in uranium ores.
uses: Dating ocean sediments in scientific research
elements.fact: Protactinium is one of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements.

elements.name: Uranium

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.note: Klaproth found its oxide in pitchblende; Eugène-Melchior Péligot isolated the metal in 1841.

elements.nameOrigin: From the planet Uranus, discovered eight years earlier.
elements.found: Mined as uraninite (pitchblende) and other ores, mainly in Kazakhstan, Canada and Australia.
uses: Once used to color glass yellow-green and ceramic glazes orange
elements.fact: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 when uranium salts fogged a wrapped photographic plate.

elements.name: Neptunium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

boil.note: An estimate; it has not been measured directly.

discovery.note: Made by hitting uranium with neutrons from a cyclotron.

elements.nameOrigin: From the planet Neptune, the next planet beyond Uranus.
elements.found: Tiny traces form in uranium ores; it is made in nuclear reactors.
elements.fact: Neptunium was the first transuranium element, the first of everything past uranium.

elements.name: Plutonium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

discovery.by: Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy and Arthur Wahl
discovery.note: Made by bombarding uranium with deuterons in a cyclotron in December 1940; identified in early 1941.

elements.nameOrigin: From the dwarf planet Pluto, following Uranus and Neptune.
elements.found: Tiny traces form in uranium ores; it is made in nuclear reactors.
uses: Plutonium-238 power sources for spacecraft such as Voyager and the Mars rovers
Fuel in some nuclear power reactors
elements.fact: The Voyager probes, launched in 1977, still run on heat from plutonium-238.

elements.name: Americium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

discovery.by: Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan and Albert Ghiorso
discovery.note: Made at the wartime Metallurgical Laboratory at the University of Chicago.

elements.nameOrigin: From the Americas, by analogy with europium above it in the table.
elements.found: Not found in nature in useful amounts; made in nuclear reactors.
uses: Gauges that measure thickness and density
elements.fact: A typical home smoke detector holds less than a millionth of a gram of americium.

elements.name: Curium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

config.note: An exception to the usual filling order, measured for the real atom.

discovery.by: Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James and Albert Ghiorso
discovery.note: Made in the Berkeley cyclotron and identified in Chicago.

elements.nameOrigin: From Marie and Pierre Curie.
elements.found: Not found in nature; made in nuclear reactors.
uses: Alpha particle sources in instruments that analyze rocks on Mars
elements.fact: The rock-analyzing instruments on several Mars rovers use curium-244.

spectrum.note: NIST lists all of these lines at one equal intensity, so their relative brightness is not known.

elements.name: Berkelium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

discovery.by: Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso and Glenn Seaborg
discovery.note: Made by bombarding americium with alpha particles.

elements.nameOrigin: From Berkeley, California, home of the lab where it was made.
elements.found: Not found in nature; made in tiny amounts in special reactors.
elements.fact: Berkelium made at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, was used to create tennessine, element 117.

spectrum.note: NIST lists all of these lines at one equal intensity, so their relative brightness is not known.

elements.name: Californium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

discovery.by: Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso and Glenn Seaborg
discovery.note: Made by bombarding curium with alpha particles.

elements.nameOrigin: From California, the state and the university.
elements.found: Not found in nature; made in tiny amounts in special reactors.
uses: Neutron sources for starting nuclear reactors
Scanning materials and finding oil and water layers in wells
elements.fact: A single microgram of californium-252 gives off millions of neutrons every second.

spectrum.note: NIST lists all of these lines at one equal intensity, so their relative brightness is not known.

elements.name: Einsteinium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

discovery.where: Berkeley, California, with Los Alamos and Argonne
discovery.note: First identified in 1952 by a team led by Albert Ghiorso; announced in 1955.

elements.nameOrigin: From Albert Einstein.
elements.found: Not found in nature; made in tiny amounts in special reactors.
elements.fact: Einsteinium is the heaviest element ever made in an amount large enough to see.

elements.name: Fermium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

elements.stateNote: Never measured; predicted to be a solid.

discovery.where: Berkeley, California, with Los Alamos and Argonne
discovery.note: First identified in 1952 alongside einsteinium; announced in 1955.

elements.nameOrigin: From Enrico Fermi.
elements.found: Not found in nature; made in reactors and accelerators in tiny amounts.
elements.fact: Fermium is the heaviest element that can be built up by adding neutrons to lighter atoms in a reactor.

spectrum.note: NIST lists no visible lines for the neutral atom; too few atoms have been studied.

elements.name: Mendelevium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

elements.stateNote: Never measured; predicted to be a solid.

discovery.by: Albert Ghiorso, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin, Stanley Thompson and Glenn Seaborg
discovery.note: Made by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles; only 17 atoms were made in the first experiments.

elements.nameOrigin: From Dmitri Mendeleev, who created the periodic table.
elements.found: Not found in nature; made in particle accelerators, only a few atoms at a time.
elements.fact: Mendelevium was the first element made and identified one atom at a time.

spectrum.note: NIST lists no visible lines for the neutral atom; too few atoms have been studied.

elements.name: Nobelium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

elements.stateNote: Never measured; predicted to be a solid.

discovery.note: Earlier claims from Sweden (1957) and Berkeley (1958) were not confirmed; Dubna's work was credited.

elements.nameOrigin: From Alfred Nobel, founder of the Nobel Prizes.
elements.found: Not found in nature; made in particle accelerators, only a few atoms at a time.
elements.fact: The name nobelium, proposed by the Swedish team whose claim failed, was kept anyway.

spectrum.note: NIST lists no visible lines for the neutral atom; too few atoms have been studied.

elements.name: Lawrencium

weight.note: No standard atomic weight; the mass number of the longest-lived known isotope is shown.

config.note: The outer electron sits in 7p rather than 6d, as NIST lists it; a 2015 measurement of its ionization energy supports this.

elements.stateNote: Never measured; predicted to be a solid.

discovery.by: Albert Ghiorso, Torbjørn Sikkeland, Almon Larsh and Robert Latimer
discovery.note: Credit was later shared with the laboratory at Dubna.

elements.nameOrigin: From Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.
